claim: Squamous cell carcinoma frequently invades as multicellular units.
source: Cancers, such as squamous cell carcinoma, frequently invade as multicellular units.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma.

claim: Invading multicellular units can be organized in a variety of ways, ranging from thin discontinuous strands to thick 'pushing' collectives.
source: However, these invading units can be organised in a variety of ways, ranging from thin discontinuous strands to thick 'pushing' collectives.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Matrix proteolysis is linked to the formation of wide strands but has little effect on the maximum extent of invasion.
source: We find that matrix proteolysis is linked to the formation of wide strands but has little effect on the maximum extent of invasion.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by computational modeling and experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Cell-cell junctions favor wide strands.
source: Cell-cell junctions also favour wide strands, but our analysis also reveals a requirement for cell-cell junctions for efficient invasion in response to uniform directional cues.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: Cell-cell junctions are required for efficient invasion in response to uniform directional cues.
source: Cell-cell junctions also favour wide strands, but our analysis also reveals a requirement for cell-cell junctions for efficient invasion in response to uniform directional cues.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by computational modeling shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The ability to generate wide invasive strands is coupled to the ability to grow effectively when surrounded by extracellular matrix in three-dimensional assays.
source: Unexpectedly, the ability to generate wide invasive strands is coupled to the ability to grow effectively when surrounded by extracellular matrix in three-dimensional assays.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 8.

claim: The most aggressive cancer behavior, both in terms of invasion and growth, is achieved at high levels of cell-cell adhesion and high levels of proteolysis.
source: Combinatorial perturbation of both matrix proteolysis and cell-cell adhesion demonstrates that the most aggressive cancer behaviour, both in terms of invasion and growth, is achieved at high levels of cell-cell adhesion and high levels of proteolysis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 7 and 9.

claim: Cells with canonical mesenchymal traits (no cell-cell junctions and high proteolysis) exhibit reduced growth and lymph node metastasis.
source: Contrary to expectation, cells with canonical mesenchymal traits – no cell-cell junctions and high proteolysis – exhibit reduced growth and lymph node metastasis.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by in vivo experimental data in Figure 9.

claim: The ability of squamous cell carcinoma cells to invade effectively is linked to their ability to generate space for proliferation in confined contexts.
source: Thus, we conclude that the ability of squamous cell carcinoma cells to invade effectively is also linked to their ability to generate space for proliferation in confined contexts.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 8.

claim: Different patterns of invasion were observed in different regions of the same tumor.
source: Interestingly, different patterns of invasion were observed in different regions of the same tumour (Figure 1a).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1a showing H&E staining of human SCC.

claim: Invasive patterns in squamous cell carcinoma range from broad 'pushing' invasive masses to thinner strands of cells to single-cell width strands.
source: These ranged from broad 'pushing' invasive masses of cells (box I), thinner strands of cells (box II), to single-cell width strands and apparently isolated single cells (box III - although this could not be definitively determined from single H&E (Hematoxylin and Eosin) sections).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: High neighbour numbers (typically 4-7) indicate broad invasion patterns.
source: Quantitative analysis of the number of cell neighbours provided a more objective metric of invasion type, with high neighbour numbers (typically 4–7) indicating broad invasion patterns and low neighbour numbers (2 or 3) indicating thin strand-like invasion, respectively (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and quantified in Figure 1b.

claim: Low neighbour numbers (2 or 3) indicate thin strand-like invasion.
source: Quantitative analysis of the number of cell neighbours provided a more objective metric of invasion type, with high neighbour numbers (typically 4–7) indicating broad invasion patterns and low neighbour numbers (2 or 3) indicating thin strand-like invasion, respectively (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and quantified in Figure 1b.

claim: Strand thickness does not fall into distinct categories, with neighbour number varying continuously between 1 and 9.
source: Analysis of neighbour number suggested that strand thickness does not fall into distinct categories, with neighbour number varying continuously between 1 and 9.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of histological data.

claim: Time-lapse imaging of primary patient explants revealed a variety of behaviors, including single-cell 'follow the leader' migration through to large 'dome-like' multi-cellular invasion.
source: Similar to the diversity observed in histological sections, this revealed a variety of behaviours, including single-cell 'follow the leader' migration through to large 'dome-like' multi-cellular invasion, even in samples from a single patient (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1c showing time-lapse microscopy.

claim: In larger invading structures, there was movement both in the direction of invasion and retrograde back to the main bulk of the explant.
source: Cell tracking revealed that, in the larger invading structures, there was movement both in the direction of invasion and retrograde back to the main bulk of the explant.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on cell tracking analysis shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The diversity of collective invasion phenotype within a single tumor suggests that the type of collective invasion is not irreversibly determined by early events in the history of the tumor.
source: The diversity of collective invasion phenotype within a single tumour suggests that the type of collective invasion is not irreversibly determined by early events in the history of the tumour but can be influenced by variations in cell state that may occur later in tumorigenesis or local environmental differences.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the text based on the observation of diverse invasion patterns within single tumors.

claim: The type of collective invasion can be influenced by variations in cell state that may occur later in tumorigenesis or local environmental differences.
source: The diversity of collective invasion phenotype within a single tumour suggests that the type of collective invasion is not irreversibly determined by early events in the history of the tumour but can be influenced by variations in cell state that may occur later in tumorigenesis or local environmental differences.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the text based on the observation of diverse invasion patterns within single tumors.

claim: A cellular Potts model was developed that incorporated both SCC cells and stromal fibroblasts.
source: Alongside these two experimental contexts, we developed a cellular Potts model that incorporated both SCC cells and stromal fibroblasts.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the computational modeling approach.

claim: The model included parameters for cancer cell-cancer cell adhesion, cancer cell-matrix adhesion, cancer cell-fibroblast adhesion, fibroblast-matrix adhesion, cell intrinsic motility, matrix displacement, and matrix proteolysis.
source: To determine whether such a change might be favourable, the model included parameters that we anticipated would influence cancer cell invasion, including cancer cell–cancer cell adhesion, cancer cell–matrix adhesion, cancer cell–fibroblast adhesion, fibroblast–matrix adhesion, cell intrinsic motility, matrix displacement, and matrix proteolysis.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the parameters included in the computational model.

claim: Effective invasion in experimental models required the addition of CAFs.
source: Experimental analysis using A431 SCC cells demonstrated that effective invasion required the addition of CAFs and, in both cases, the invasion was almost entirely collective (Figure 2b panels iii and vi).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2b showing experimental invasion assays.

claim: Invasion in experimental models was almost entirely collective.
source: Experimental analysis using A431 SCC cells demonstrated that effective invasion required the addition of CAFs and, in both cases, the invasion was almost entirely collective (Figure 2b panels iii and vi).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2b.

claim: The in silico model replicated the fibroblast-dependent invasion observed in both organotypic and spheroid assays.
source: This enabled the in silico replication of the fibroblast-dependent invasion observed in both organotypic and spheroid assays (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2b comparing model outputs to experimental data.

claim: The extent of increased invasion scaled with the number of fibroblasts.
source: In line with previous experimental reports (Gaggioli et al., 2007), the extent of increased invasion scaled with the number of fibroblasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to previous work and illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: PCA revealed a wide and continuous spread of invasion patterns.
source: PCA revealed a wide and continuous spread of invasion patterns, with the first two dimensions of the PCA accounting for 75% (organotypic) and 65% (spheroid) of the variation (Appendix 3 – table 1 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on PCA analysis of model outputs.

claim: There was no indication of discrete sub-classes of invasive pattern, suggesting a continuous spectrum of invasive behaviours.
source: Notably, there was no indication of discrete sub-classes of invasive pattern, suggesting a continuous spectrum of invasive behaviours.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on PCA analysis of model outputs.

claim: The continuous spectrum implied by PCA was in line with the range of invasive strand geometries observed in clinical muSCC samples.
source: The continuous spectrum implied by PCA was in line with the range of invasive strand geometries observed in clinical muSCC samples (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text comparing model predictions to clinical observations.

claim: Increasing cancer cell proteolysis led to only modestly elevated invasion scores in organotypic contexts.
source: Somewhat contrary to expectation, we found that increasing cancer cell proteolysis led to only modestly elevated invasion scores in organotypic contexts.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The maximum invasive depth did not correlate with matrix proteolysis.
source: Moreover, the maximum invasive depth did not correlate with matrix proteolysis (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3b showing heatmaps of model outputs.

claim: The width of the strands (neighbour numbers) increased as a function of proteolysis, especially in organotypic assays.
source: Instead the width of the strands (neighbour numbers) increased as a function of proteolysis, especially in organotypic assays.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 3b.

claim: In simulations with low proteolysis, the model predicted thin strands (low neighbour and low tapering scores).
source: In simulations with low proteolysis, the model predicted thin strands (low neighbour and low tapering scores).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on computational modeling results.

claim: Increasing proteolysis leads to reduced curvature and a 'pushing' front in the absence of a track.
source: Figure 3—figure supplement 1c shows that increasing proteolysis leads to reduced curvature and a 'pushing' front in the absence of a track.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: ECM fibres parallel to the direction of the invasive cue favoured invasion.
source: As might be expected, ECM fibres parallel to the direction of the invasive cue favoured invasion, but isotropic texture hindered invasion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d showing model simulations.

claim: Isotropic ECM texture hindered invasion.
source: As might be expected, ECM fibres parallel to the direction of the invasive cue favoured invasion, but isotropic texture hindered invasion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: High proteolysis reduces the maximal extent of invasion but increases the strand width in spheroid assays.
source: Analysis of spheroid contexts yielded a different picture, with reduced maximum invasion depth with increasing proteolysis values.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The very highest matrix degradation value yielded significantly lower maximum invasion depth than the intermediate and lowest level in spheroid contexts.
source: Notably, the very highest matrix degradation value yielded significantly lower maximum invasion depth than the intermediate and lowest level.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 3b.

claim: MMP14 over-expression increased the proteolysis of collagen.
source: In line with expectation, MMP14 over-expression increased the proteolysis of collagen, while MMP14 deletion reduced proteolysis (as assessed by DQ collagen fluorescence) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1g showing DQ collagen assays.

claim: MMP14 deletion reduced collagen proteolysis.
source: In line with expectation, MMP14 over-expression increased the proteolysis of collagen, while MMP14 deletion reduced proteolysis (as assessed by DQ collagen fluorescence) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1g.

claim: The maximum invasion depth in the organotypic context did not simply increase with MMP14 levels, with strand lengths similar between MMP14 KO and over-expressing cells.
source: In particular, the maximum invasion depth in the organotypic context did not simply increase with MMP14 levels, with strand lengths similar between MMP14 KO and over-expressing cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on experimental data shown in Figure 3c and d.

claim: The strand width was notably affected by MMP14 levels in both organotypic and spheroid assays, with KO cells generating thin strands and over-expressing cells generating thick strands.
source: In contrast, the strand width was notably affected by MMP14 levels in both organotypic and spheroid assays (yellow lines in Figure 3c indicate strand width), with KO cells generating thin strands and over-expressing cells generating thick strands.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3c and d.

claim: The positive relationship between ECM proteolysis and strand width was particularly strong in organotypic contexts.
source: The positive relationship between ECM proteolysis and strand width was particularly strong in organotypic contexts (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3c and d.

claim: Matrix proteolysis promoted wide strands even if cancer cell proliferation was prevented by pre-treatment with mitomycin C.
source: Of note, matrix proteolysis promoted wide strands even if cancer cell proliferation was prevented by pre-treatment with mitomycin C (Figure 3—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1h.

claim: MMP14 is a major determinant of the mode of collective cancer cell invasion but plays little role in determining the maximum distance invaded.
source: These results are highly concordant with the model predictions and confirm that MMP14 is a major determinant of the mode of collective cancer cell invasion but plays little role in determining the maximum distance invaded.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on combined computational and experimental results.

claim: There was no consistent association between cancer cell-matrix adhesion and invasive pattern in the organotypic context.
source: There was no consistent association between cancer cell-matrix adhesion and invasive pattern in the organotypic context, with high adhesion values distributed across the PCA plot.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on PCA analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The relationship between cell-matrix adhesion and invasion score was relatively flat, with only very high cell-matrix adhesion values boosting invasion.
source: The relationship between cell-matrix adhesion and invasion score was relatively flat, with only very high cell-matrix adhesion values boosting invasion.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 4b.

claim: ITGB1 deletion had no effect on cancer invasion in the experimental organotypic model.
source: This prediction is supported by the lack of effect of ITGB1 deletion on cancer invasion in the experimental organotypic model (Figure 4c and d – Figure 4—figure supplement 1b and c confirm that ITGB1 KO cells are defective in collagen I and Matrigel adhesion).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 4c and d.

claim: In the spheroid context, there was a somewhat stronger association between matrix adhesion and invasion.
source: In the spheroid context, there was a somewhat stronger association between matrix adhesion and invasion.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The strongest correlation between matrix adhesion and invasion was with the tapering metric that reflects whether strands have a uniform breadth or taper as they invade deeper.
source: Intriguingly, the strongest correlation was with the tapering metric that reflects whether strands have a uniform breadth or taper as they invade deeper (Figure 4b – row 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 4b.

claim: Greater tapering was observed in ITGB1 KO spheroids.
source: Greater tapering observed in ITGB1 KO spheroids (Figure 4c and d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 4c and d.

claim: Tapering in ITGB1 KO cells was not observed in organotypic assays.
source: Interestingly, and in line with model predictions, this was not observed in organotypic assays (Figure 4b–d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 4b-d.

claim: Reducing cancer cell-cancer cell adhesion reduced the total invasion score in organotypic assays across relatively large ranges of parameter space.
source: First, reducing cancer cell–cancer cell adhesion reduced the total invasion score in organotypic assays across relatively large ranges of parameter space (Figure 5a and b – note the association of increasing magenta intensity and invasion score vectors in the PCA plot).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 5a and b.

claim: In organotypic contexts, lower cancer cell-cancer cell adhesion resulted in shorter invasive strands that thinned rapidly as they invaded.
source: Specifically, in organotypic contexts, lower cancer cell–cancer cell adhesion resulted in shorter invasive strands that thinned rapidly as they invaded (this is reflected in the Max. Invasion, Mean Neighbour, and Tapering rows in Figure 5b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 5b.

claim: A431 cells lacking adherens junctions (CTNNA1 KO) were significantly less invasive, both in terms of strand length and strand width, in organotypic assays.
source: Strikingly, and, in line with the model predictions, these cells lacking adherens junctions were significantly less invasive, both in terms of strand length and strand width, in organotypic assays (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 5d.

claim: In spheroid assays, loss of α-catenin did not affect strand length and had only a modest effect on strand width (~20% reduction compared to a 60% reduction in width in organotypic assays).
source: In spheroid assays, loss of α-catenin did not affect strand length and had only a modest effect on strand width (~20% reduction compared to a 60% reduction in width in organotypic assays).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Cancer cell junctions are favourable for invasion when cells are subject to a uniform directional cue.
source: These analyses indicate that cancer cell junctions are favourable for invasion when cells are subject to a uniform directional cue.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The importance of junctions only when there is a uniform directional cue suggests that it may not be cell-cell adhesion per se that is important but some linkage between cell-cell adhesions and coordination of collective invasion.
source: The importance of junctions only when there is a uniform directional cue suggests that it may not be cell-cell adhesion per se that is important but some linkage between cell-cell adhesions and coordination of collective invasion.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the text based on modeling results.

claim: Cadherin-mediated coordination of actin and myosin dynamics is important for effective collective migration of neural crest cells during cranio-facial development and for border cell migration in the Drosophila egg chamber.
source: Consistent with this idea, cadherin-mediated coordination of actin and myosin dynamics is important for effective collective migration of neural crest cells during cranio-facial development and for border cell migration in the Drosophila egg chamber (Geisbrecht and Montell, 2002; Shellard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to previous work.

claim: Control A431 cells exhibit supra-cellular organisation of their actomyosin network.
source: Figure 6a confirms control A431 cells exhibit supra-cellular organisation of their actomyosin network (Hidalgo-Carcedo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to previous work and illustrated in Figure 6a.

claim: Knockout of CTNNA1 disrupts the formation of a supra-cellular actomyosin network.
source: Furthermore, knockout of CTNNA1 disrupts the formation of a supra-cellular actomyosin network (Figure 6a – quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 6a.

claim: CTNNB1 failed to localise to cell-cell contacts in CTNNA1 KO A431 cells.
source: As expected, CTNNB1 failed to localise to cell-cell contacts in CTNNA1 KO A431 cells (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 6a.

claim: ROCK:ER boosts actomyosin contractility throughout the cytoplasm including at cell-cell interfaces in the presence of 4OHT.
source: In the presence of 4OHT, ROCK:ER boosts actomyosin contractility throughout the cytoplasm including at cell-cell interfaces (Croft et al., 2004), and the latter reduces the activity of the supra-cellular actomyosin belt.
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to previous work.

claim: ROCK kinase inhibition reduces the activity of the supra-cellular actomyosin belt.
source: In the presence of 4OHT, ROCK:ER boosts actomyosin contractility throughout the cytoplasm including at cell-cell interfaces (Croft et al., 2004), and the latter reduces the activity of the supra-cellular actomyosin belt.
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: Both ROCK:ER activation and ROCK kinase inhibition reduce the width of invading strands.
source: Figure 6d and e shows that both manipulations reduce the width of invading strands, demonstrating that disrupting actomyosin coordination mechanisms phenocopy loss of adherens junctions with respect to the width of invading strands (note: for this experiment we used ECM pre-conditioned by fibroblasts in the absence of drug and then added cancer cells in the presence of the indicated perturbations).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 6d and e.

claim: Disrupting actomyosin coordination mechanisms phenocopy loss of adherens junctions with respect to the width of invading strands.
source: Figure 6d and e shows that both manipulations reduce the width of invading strands, demonstrating that disrupting actomyosin coordination mechanisms phenocopy loss of adherens junctions with respect to the width of invading strands (note: for this experiment we used ECM pre-conditioned by fibroblasts in the absence of drug and then added cancer cells in the presence of the indicated perturbations).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 6d and e.

claim: Adherens junctions influence invasive pattern by enabling supra-cellular coordination of actomyosin, and not simply determining whether cancer cells are able to maintain contact with one another.
source: Furthermore, the data support a model in which adherens junctions influence invasive pattern by enabling supra-cellular coordination of actomyosin, and not simply determining whether cancer cells are able to maintain contact with one another.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on experimental data.

claim: The high neighbour number observed when matrix proteolysis is high would depend upon cell-cell junctions in organotypic assays.
source: Potts modelling predicted that the high neighbour number observed when matrix proteolysis is high would depend upon cell-cell junctions in organotypic assays (note the higher values in the top right regions on the plots in Figure 7ai).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 7a.

claim: The cooperative interaction between proteolysis and cell-cell adhesion was not predicted to influence the extent of maximum invasion, which was dominated by cell-cell adhesion alone.
source: Interestingly, this cooperative interaction between proteolysis and cell-cell adhesion was not predicted to influence the extent of maximum invasion, which was dominated by cell-cell adhesion alone (Figure 7aii).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 7a.

claim: Deletion of CTTNA1 prevented the formation of wide invasive strands by MMP14 over-expressing A431 cells in the organotypic invasion assays.
source: These predictions were supported by experimentation: deletion of CTTNA1 prevented the formation of wide invasive strands by MMP14 over-expressing A431 cells in the organotypic invasion assays (Figure 7c), with more subtle effects observed in the spheroid assays (Figure 7a, d, and e).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 7c.

claim: If both ECM proteolysis and cell-cell adhesion are high then a broad, virtually flat, invasive front is generated.
source: Figure 7—figure supplement 1a and b shows that if both ECM proteolysis and cell-cell adhesion are high then a broad, virtually flat, invasive front is generated.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 7—figure supplement 1a and b.

claim: Reducing either proteolysis or cell-cell adhesion leads to increased curvature of the invasive front.
source: Reducing either proteolysis or cell-cell adhesion leads to increased curvature.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: A broad 'pushing' front of invasion requires both high proteolysis and high cancer cell-cancer cell adhesion.
source: Together, these analyses establish that a broad 'pushing' front of invasion requires both high proteolysis and high cancer cell–cancer cell adhesion.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on combined computational and experimental results.

claim: The vectors reflecting cell growth and neighbour number in the PCA analysis were closely aligned.
source: Interestingly, the vectors reflecting cell growth and neighbour number in the PCA analysis were closely aligned (Figure 2c and d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2c and d.

claim: Proliferating cells were observed throughout spheroids.
source: EdU staining revealed that proliferating cells were observed throughout spheroids (Figure 8—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 8—figure supplement 1a and b.

claim: There was a positive association between the proportion of EdU positive cells in invading strands and the strand width.
source: Moreover, there was a positive association between the proportion of EdU positive cells in invading strands and the strand width.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on EdU staining analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1a and b.

claim: The linkage between strand widening and growth was particularly pronounced in the spheroid simulations lacking fibroblasts.
source: The modelling indicated that the linkage between strand widening and growth was particularly pronounced in the spheroid simulations lacking fibroblasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1f.

claim: Neither proteolysis nor cancer cell-cancer cell adhesion was predicted to have a strong effect on cell growth in organotypic assays, either in the presence or absence of CAFs.
source: Neither was predicted to have a strong effect on cell growth in organotypic assays, either in the presence or absence of CAFs (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 8a.

claim: A strong positive relationship between proteolysis and growth was predicted in the context of spheroids lacking CAFs.
source: In contrast, a strong positive relationship between proteolysis and growth was predicted in the context of spheroids lacking CAFs (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 8a.

claim: Cancer cell-cancer cell adhesions were predicted to make a positive contribution to growth, albeit smaller than the effect of proteolysis.
source: Cancer cell–cancer cell adhesions were also predicted to make a positive contribution to growth, albeit smaller than the effect of proteolysis (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 8a.

claim: Manipulation of MMP14 and CTTNA1 had minimal effect on cell growth in unconfined two-dimensional (2D) culture conditions.
source: Manipulation of MMP14 and CTTNA1 had minimal effect on cell growth in unconfined two-dimensional (2D) culture conditions (Figure 8—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 8—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Both proteolysis and cancer cell-cancer cell adhesion are required for effective cell growth in 3D collagen matrices.
source: Figure 8b and c confirms that both proteolysis and cancer cell–cancer cell adhesion are required for effective cell growth in 3D collagen matrices.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 8b and c.

claim: The positive effect of boosting proteolysis required cell-cell adhesions.
source: Moreover, the positive effect of boosting proteolysis required cell-cell adhesions (Figure 8b and c compares MMP14 OE with αCATKO MMP14 OE).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 8b and c.

claim: Ectopic activation of ROCK2, which disrupts cytoskeletal cohesion in cell clusters, reduced growth in 3D collagen.
source: Ectopic activation of ROCK2, which disrupts cytoskeletal cohesion in cell clusters, also reduced growth in 3D collagen (Figure 8—figure supplement 1d and e).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 8—figure supplement 1d and e.

claim: ECM displacement was observed directly in time-lapse movies and as the formation and compaction of ECM fibres at the cancer cell-ECM interface.
source: This was observed directly in time-lapse movies and as the formation and compaction of ECM fibres at the cancer cell-ECM interface (note arrows in Figure 8e and f).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 8e and f.

claim: Highly dynamic membrane blebs and filopodia were observed at the cancer cell-ECM interface.
source: These analyses also revealed highly dynamic membrane blebs and filopodia at the cancer cell-ECM interface.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on imaging analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: ECM compaction was absent when CTNNA1 KO cells were used.
source: ECM compaction was absent when CTNNA1 KO cells were used.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on imaging analysis shown in Figure 8f.

claim: MMP over-expression reduced ECM compaction and led to the formation of gaps in the ECM adjacent to the cancer cells with reduced numbers of membrane blebs.
source: MMP over-expression reduced ECM compaction and led to the formation of gaps in the ECM adjacent to the cancer cells with reduced numbers of membrane blebs (Figure 8f).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 8f.

claim: MMP14 over-expressing cells generated tumors with particularly wide, bulging, margins.
source: Of note, MMP over-expressing cells generated tumours with particularly wide, bulging, margins (Figure 9a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 9a.

claim: There was a strong correlation between the levels of MMP14 and tumour growth.
source: Strikingly, there was a strong correlation between the levels of MMP14 and tumour growth (Figure 9b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 9b.

claim: In MMP14 over-expressing tumours, clusters of SCC cells distant from the main tumour were larger, rounder (as judged by aspect ratio), and further from the tumour.
source: Histological analysis revealed clusters of SCC cells in the ear distant from the main tumour. In MMP14 over-expressing tumours, these clusters were larger, rounder (as judged by aspect ratio), and further from the tumour (Figure 9—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 9—figure supplement 1a and b.

claim: Metastatic spread to lymph nodes correlated with MMP14 levels.
source: Metastatic spread to lymph nodes also correlated with MMP14 levels, which are in line with previous reports (Bartolomé et al., 2009; Devy et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to previous work and supported by data in Figure 9c.

claim: Reducing cancer cell-cancer cell adhesion did not lead to a more aggressive tumour phenotype but reduced both tumour growth, and very few mice were observed to have lymph node metastases.
source: Notably, and in contrast to the prevailing dogma, reducing cancer cell–cancer cell adhesion did not lead to a more aggressive tumour phenotype but reduced both tumour growth, and very few mice were observed to have lymph node metastases (Figure 9c).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 9c.

claim: The defect in CTNNA1 KO cells could be partly compensated by over-expression of MMP14.
source: This could be partly compensated by over-expression of MMP14, suggesting that a defect in 'space' generation might underpin the defect in the CTNNA1 KO cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The growth and lymph node metastasis of MMP14 o.e./CTNNA1 KO cells were reduced compared to the MMP14 o.e. cells.
source: However, the growth and lymph node metastasis of MMP14 o.e./CTNNA1 KO cells were reduced compared to the MMP14 o.e. cells (Figure 9c), indicating that the tumour promoting effect of elevated MMP14 levels depends on cell-cell adhesion.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 9c.

claim: MMP14-driven matrix proteolysis promotes invasion in wide collective units and tumour growth in spatially confined contexts.
source: Together, these analyses demonstrate that MMP14-driven matrix proteolysis promotes invasion in wide collective units and tumour growth in spatially confined contexts.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on in vivo experimental data.

claim: The widening of invasive units, tumour growth, and lymph node metastases depends upon adherens junction-mediated supra-cellular coordination of the actomyosin network.
source: Furthermore, the widening of invasive units, tumour growth, and lymph node metastases depends upon adherens junction-mediated supra-cellular coordination of the actomyosin network.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on combined experimental results.

claim: Collective seeding of metastases is more efficient than single cell seeding.
source: The importance of collective invasion is underscored by several recent studies showing that collective seeding of metastases is more efficient than single cell seeding (Cheung et al., 2016; Fischer et al., 2015; Khalil et al., 2017; Padmanaban et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to previous work.

claim: E-cadherin/CDH1 and P-cadherin/CDH3 are the predominant cadherins in mucosal squamous cell carcinomas.
source: E-cadherin/CDH1 and, to a lesser extent, P-cadherin/CDH3 are the predominant cadherins in mucosal squamous cell carcinomas (SCC or muSCC specifically for mucosal SCC; Nieman et al., 1999) that typically do not undergo a clear epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to previous work.

claim: Cadherins are coupled to the actin cytoskeleton via a complex containing α-catenin and β-catenin.
source: These cadherins are coupled to the actin cytoskeleton via a complex containing α-catenin and β-catenin (Nelson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to previous work.

claim: ITGB1 is particularly highly expressed in SCC.
source: This is primarily mediated by integrin receptors (Hamidi and Ivaska, 2018; Janes and Watt, 2006), with ITGB1 particularly highly expressed in SCC (Janes and Watt, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to previous work.

claim: The ECM presents a barrier to migration if the gaps between fibres are smaller than 3-5 μm.
source: The ECM presents a barrier to migration if the gaps between fibres are smaller than 3–5 μm (Wolf et al., 2013; Wolf et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to previous work.

claim: The dermal ECM underlying SCC lesions is predominantly composed of type I collagen.
source: The dermal ECM underlying SCC lesions is predominantly composed of type I collagen (Watt and Fujiwara, 2011), and numerous studies have demonstrated that MMP14/MT-1MMP is the critical protease for degrading this type of matrix (Castro-Castro et al., 2016; Gifford and Itoh, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to previous work.

claim: MMP14/MT-1MMP is the critical protease for degrading type I collagen matrix.
source: The dermal ECM underlying SCC lesions is predominantly composed of type I collagen (Watt and Fujiwara, 2011), and numerous studies have demonstrated that MMP14/MT-1MMP is the critical protease for degrading this type of matrix (Castro-Castro et al., 2016; Gifford and Itoh, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to previous work.

claim: Stromal cells are the major source of both matrix proteolytic and force-mediated matrix remodelling in tumours.
source: In many cases, stromal cells are the major source of both matrix proteolytic and force-mediated matrix remodelling in tumours (Conklin and Keely, 2012; Kalluri and Zeisberg, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to previous work.

claim: Cancer-associated fibroblasts can promote the invasion of SCC by providing matrix remodeling functions and are frequently observed leading the migration of cancer cells that retain epithelial characteristics.
source: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs, sometimes referred to as stromal fibroblasts) can promote the invasion of SCC by providing these functions and are frequently observed leading the migration of cancer cells that retain epithelial characteristics (Gaggioli et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to previous work.
